title: Reproducing Transparent and Scrutable Recommendations: Exploring Open-Weight Models via Natural-Language User Profiles
summary: In this reproducibility study, we investigate the transparency and scrutability of recommender systems enhanced by incorporating generated natural-language user profiles that represent user preferences. The original paper explores the synthesis of user profiles from raw user-generated review text across domains such as movies and accommodations (Amazon Movies & TV, TripAdvisor). Crucially, these natural-language user profiles enable direct user interaction and intervention, allowing users to customize recommendations by correcting misattributed preferences or addressing cold-start settings. We successfully reproduce the core findings of the original study. Additionally, we extend the evaluation by conducting systematic context ablation experiments, multi-seed stability across five distinct random seeds to establish statistical reliability, and a mechanistic interpretability analysis using the nnsight framework to probe internal model representations under counterfactual profile perturbations. Our findings verify the original paper's claim that User Profile Recommendation (UPR) achieves competitive performance under its test-set reranking protocol and makes recommendations more transparent. Perturbing the natural-language profiles does change predictions, but it shifts predicted ratings uniformly across genres with no detectable genre-selective effect, leaving rankings unchanged even under direct activation steering. We trace this back to the rating-regression objective rather than the profile interface, with ranking-objective models clearly exceeding in this task.
comment: Accepted at BlackBoxNLP@EMNLP'26 (The 9th BlackboxNLP Workshop Special Track: Reproducibility and Reliability in Interpretability Analyses)

AI.tldr: This is a reproducibility study of the original User Profile Recommendation (UPR) work that uses open-weight models with natural language user profiles for transparent recommender systems. The authors successfully reproduce the original core findings, conduct additional extended evaluations including ablation experiments, stability testing and mechanistic interpretability analysis, and find that the rating-regression objective of UPR limits the effectiveness of profile perturbation for controllable ranking, while ranking-objective models perform better on this task.
AI.motivation: Transparency and scrutability are important properties for recommender systems. The original work proposed UPR that uses generated natural-language user profiles to enable user interaction and intervention for more transparent recommendations. This study aims to reproduce the core findings of the original work, verify its conclusions, and extend the evaluation with additional analyses to further understand the mechanism of UPR.
AI.method: 1. Reproduce the core experiments of the original UPR study on public datasets (Amazon Movies & TV, TripAdvisor). 2. Extend evaluation with systematic context ablation experiments, multi-seed stability tests across 5 random seeds for statistical reliability, and mechanistic interpretability analysis via the nnsight framework to probe internal model representations under counterfactual profile perturbations.
AI.result: 1. The original core finding that UPR achieves competitive performance under test-set reranking and improves recommendation transparency is successfully verified. 2. Perturbing natural-language user profiles changes predicted ratings but causes uniform shifts across genres without detectable genre-selective effects, so rankings remain unchanged even under direct activation steering. 3. This limitation is caused by UPR's rating-regression objective, and ranking-objective models perform significantly better on controllable recommendation via profile perturbation.
AI.conclusion: The original conclusions of UPR are reproducible, but the limited controllability of recommendation ranking via profile perturbation in UPR stems from its rating-regression training objective. Using a ranking objective instead can improve the controllability and scrutability of natural language profile-based recommender systems.

title: A Policy Profile for Croissant: Refusal as a Property of the Dataset
summary: Croissant is the de facto machine-readable descriptor for ML datasets: JSON-LD over schema.org. Since version 1.1 it also carries data use conditions, recommending DUO and ODRL for them. What no version specifies is how any of them is evaluated: no decision procedure, no bound on evaluation cost, no outcome for a condition an implementation cannot evaluate, no record of what was checked, and nothing on composition with caller-side authority. We supply that half. An additive profile lets a dataset declare the operations it admits and the conditions under which it admits them, over a closed set of five operators whose decision procedure is given in full, so a gate decides from the descriptor alone and records what it checked. Two corpora evaluate it and their evidence is kept apart. Three descriptors that gated a real nf-core pipeline give the deployment result: decisions from a profile document match the gate's native descriptor record for record, stripping the layer leaves a valid Croissant document, and the added cost is 11.7 $μ$s against a 119 $μ$s decision. A corpus generated from the profile's grammar gives the breadth, covering every operator, refusal class and conformance clause. Across its valid cases, 552 complete decision records agree three ways -- native descriptor, profile terms, and the same policy as ODRL in usageInfo. The carrier is therefore not the contribution; the evaluation semantics is. Finally, caller-bound and data-bound policies range over non-overlapping state spaces, so neither permit set contains the other.
comment: 23 pages. Reference implementation and conformance corpus archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22018156 and doi:10.5281/zenodo.22016112

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an additive policy profile for the Croissant ML dataset descriptor standard to address the lack of specified evaluation procedures for data use conditions, defining clear decision semantics, evaluating the profile on real pipelines and synthetic corpora, and confirming its effectiveness with low overhead.
AI.motivation: While Croissant is the de facto machine-readable descriptor for ML datasets and supports data use conditions since v1.1, no version of Croissant specifies how these conditions should be evaluated: there is no decision procedure, no bound on evaluation cost, no handling of unevaluable conditions, no check records, and no guidance for composition with caller-side authority, creating a gap that needs to be filled.
AI.method: The authors propose an additive policy profile that lets datasets declare admitted operations and their corresponding conditions based on a closed set of five operators with fully specified decision procedures. A gate mechanism makes decisions directly from the descriptor and records checks. The profile is evaluated on two corpora: a real deployment with three descriptors for an nf-core pipeline, and a synthetic corpus covering all operators, refusal classes and conformance clauses generated from the profile's grammar.
AI.result: In real deployment, decisions from the profile document match the gate's native descriptor records 1:1, the resulting document remains a valid Croissant after stripping the profile layer, and the added overhead is only 11.7 microseconds against a baseline 119 microsecond decision. All 552 valid cases in the synthetic corpus show three-way agreement between native descriptors, profile terms, and the same policy represented as ODRL in usageInfo. It is also found that caller-bound and data-bound policies occupy non-overlapping state spaces with neither's permit set containing the other.
AI.conclusion: The key contribution of this work is the addition of complete evaluation semantics for data use conditions in Croissant, not the carrier format. The proposed profile effectively fills the gap in Croissant, works correctly with low overhead, and is compatible with existing Croissant standards.
